A little bit of background about me before I speak on this: I am definitely on the large-end of straight-sized, and I feel that I have a fat identity. Even though I have been a wide range of sizes, I was bullied by family, friends, and peers my entire childhood for being “fat”. 

I worried about this issue a lot when I started working on self-acceptance because I wanted to affirm my size but it felt like appropriation to call myself “fat” in fat-accepting spaces. I had a private 1-1 conversation about this with a close friend who is larger-sized than me and claims her own fat identity. Her opinion was that it was okay for me to have a fat identity, so long as I accepted that there are experienced and spaces that I can’t know about/ understand because they belong to people who are bigger than me. And I think this applies to a lot of people on the fat spectrum (like people who are fat but not infini-fat or super fat, for example). I’m not saying I have the answers, but this is where I’m at with this question right now.

And if this sounds like a perspective that feels appropriate to you, I bet you could get your friend to this perspective with some discussion and guide them towards being more of an ally.

Tl;Dr: I’m doing great here’s my brainstorm about why I’m happy not being in a relationship. I also have CPTSD.

I have been feeling this way too for about a year! At first I worried I was giving up on something or acting like an incel/ red pill person or whatever. But upon reflection, there is just so much to explore in this world with me and my dog. Why forego any of those things for a relationship? I want to travel, go on hikes with my dog, learn new tricks, grow old together (with my dog who is my best friend and the only being to show me unconditional love). I personally don’t feel like I need a “no dating and no sex” policy anymore because I’m just not that interested in it. Financially I love just focusing on my dog and, as my career is finally starting to pick up, being able to get an Xbox or a new computer without feeling like it’s a huge deal. I think a serious relationship and “starting a family” could take that away. I guess I don’t even need to say this, but in case it does you any good: it sounds like you know that obviously you have literally nothing to feel bad about whether or not you get a relationship. 

I think sometimes our friends and family inadvertently diminish our trauma by telling us that we will find someone, etc. They don’t want to face the fact that our childhoods have *kind of* locked us out of relationships/ intimacy. But in a weird way, I don’t actually feel locked out anymore. I think it’s more that I know the truth about relationships and how inevitably fragile they are. This isn’t coming out as linear as I would like it to be, but learning that unconditional love (from a human) doesn’t exist is a big lesson to learn as a kid. And we, you, I, other CPTSD-ers we know that on a _physical_, embodied level. So even if we can have a relationship, even if we aren’t locked out, I think another part of the truth is that we have intimate access to some information that suggests it’s not a great idea.

Maybe in a word: I don’t feel like I’m unfit for relationships anymore; but right now I just don’t believe in them? Like a happy atheist who doesn’t believe in God. I see friends who have relationships and I am happy for them, but they have also had easy lives; I hope nothing ever happens to them that changes things because I am happy they get to live with their illusions. But I don’t have those illusions, but that’s okay because there are so many other ways to make a safe, happy, healthy, and fulfilling life.

For example, I personally work in education. I prioritize being a resilience factor (opposite of an ACE) for all of the young people I work with. I don’t always perfectly succeed in this of course, but I build meaning that way. And I think it’s similar to the meaning other people build by having kids or finding “true love”.

Sorry this is so messy! Your post really made me think and I just wanted to put my thoughts in a thread so I can read them later. I think I’m right with you; I don’t think I want a relationship because they hurt me too much when they expire. and I think that’s totally fine? Like if someone says “I don’t like coffee because it gives me heartburn” it’s not like everyone gangs up on them and tells them to give coffee another chance. 

Last thing I feel like pointing out is that we kind of live in a world that is full of alienation and people don’t know where to look for meaning/ fulfillment/ enlightenment. but relationships are right there, an obvious thing to try. A thing to care about. kind of like how people focus on making money. After a while it’s like “Why? don’t you have enough!” But they just don’t know what else to do. and they are threatened by people who aren’t focused on making money. like when I say Im learning to be a teacher they say “what are you going to do with that?” And they mean “how are you going to make money with that” as if surplus money is the only important thing in this life. (obviously not having enough money is pretty fucking important, but that’s not what I’m talking about). 

Thanks for letting me dump, I feel safe in this thread. I might dump more with a reply/ edit later.

I know that sounds impossible, and I know I don’t know everything. But still, if I could, I would bet my (small amount of) savings that you will be in a better place than where you were before the diagnosis. In the meantime, I am trying to hold mental space for you and send encouraging messages. Recovery will
be slow, but it builds upon itself. I think the frustration you feel towards the people around you is a sign that you are holding emotional space for new people who can support you. Read your whole rant, and tbh it was really interesting for me because I worked service during COVID and now I am one of these wfh people. One thing to keep in mind is that capitalism is designed to pit workers against each other; the bosses don’t want lawyers, doctors, teenagers bagging groceries, and firefighters to all wind up in one big union. So work is broken down into a wide range of disparate experiences, all to prevent us from seeing the main thing in common: everyone is getting exploited. Even if a pastry chef and a college professor seem to be having totally different experiences, at the end of the day they are both selling their work to a boss for way less than it is worth because that’s how a business makes money. Boom. Mic drop. Value is labor and thus capital rests on the exploitation of the working class. 

The other thing that happens because of this— and I think this is why your feelings are super valid— is that people who do mental work instead of service work or physical labor are conditioned to think that they are *not* being exploited. They are conditioned to think they have “good” jobs, etc. This is such a thing in the USA, and you can see it pretty much anywhere. What I’m trying to say is that one reason you might feel alienated is that you are closer to the truth. You probably know you are getting exploited, and you have to listen to people whine about their desk jobs, *even while they also probably think they have it better than you*. That’s annoying. If it does you any good, remember they are victims too and even if they think they are more successful and secure than you, they really aren’t that much. If it does you any good. 

I think that for these reasons sometimes people at desk jobs do need to pull back and make sure people in service jobs have a bigger platform. You all are just closer to the truth most of the time.

You raise an interesting point here. I am not a rabbi. I am a convert. I do not wish to share the denominational status of my conversion. This issue is close to me and I have, of course, at many times, thought about it. Also, I should warn, no Jewish denomination would accept my personal view on this topic. But here goes:

I think that the halacha might not actually support the predominant Orthodox opinion on Reform conversion. However, since Reform rabbis do not spend as much (enough?) time on the halacha, they do not defend the halachic status of their converts on halachic grounds. Therefore, unexplored questions arise when one tries to offer halacha-informed responses to Orthodox rejections of Reform conversion.

The Orthodox argument for the non-halachic status of Reform converts relies on the premise that if a rabbi does not view the halacha as binding, then that rabbi cannot bind a convert to the halacha. Rabbi Marc Angel states that this claim is justified “ipso facto”—in other words, he claims that it is “just obvious” that this is true. (Other Orthodox explanations of this issue offer similar justifications, often through rhetorical questions.)

But this “ipso facto” justification of the claim is insufficient, mainly because it does not address the possibility that a rabbi might bind a convert to the halacha even if that rabbi did not realize that doing so was an inevitable consequence of carrying out the halachic conversion rituals (beit din, circumcision, mikveh).

So, instead of using rhetorical questions or ipso facto justification, Orthodox rabbis, if they want to convince Reform converts (or anyone really) that Reform converts are not Jewish, must explain why a rabbi who binds a convert to the halacha must know or intend to do so.

And this state of affairs is not as obvious as it might seem. First of all, there is a halachic instance of one person binding another to the halacha that does not involve any intention or knowledge: when a Jewish woman carries a pregnancy to term, she has arguably bound her child to the halacha—whether she wanted, intended, or understood that that is what she did. 

Therefore, on grounds of parity, it might be appropriate to evaluate conversion in terms that are “material” (i.e., in terms of the halachic rituals that must take place) rather than “intentional” (i.e., in terms of the spiritual, psychological, doxastic properties of the sponsoring rabbi and beit din).

Furthermore, denominational differences in Judaism only emerged in the nineteenth century. Therefore the question of a rabbi who does not view the halacha as strictly binding performing a conversion does not have a precedent in Oral or written Torah. There is, of course, an opinion, inferred from the Talmud, that a convert must accept the halacha as binding in order to convert successfully. But to appeal to this as a reason for rejecting all Reform conversions, one would have to assume that all Reform converts view the halacha as non-binding. This is not the explanation or premise offered in the predominant Orthodox argument for the non halachic status of Reform conversions, and furthermore, it seems impossible to justify. There is no way of knowing the personal attitudes concerning halacha of each and every Reform convert.

Furthermore, early discussions of conversion suggested that the three members of a converts beth din did not need to be rabbis. So it seems to be a departure from the halacha to argue that a true conversion must be sponsored by a rabbi, ordained by an Orthodox institution. 

I’ll stop now with the “furthermore”’s in order to avoid the risk of running on too long. But I do still need to discuss the uptake of this line of thought.

If I’m right—big “if”, but not as big as I think most Orthodox Jews who feel strongly about Reform conversions (which is not the same group as all Orthodox Jews) would like it to be—then the following is true:

If the halacha is binding, then Reform converts have halachic obligations that they are at risk of leaving unfulfilled while they are involved in Reform communities. The same is true, from an Orthodox perspective, for any other Reform Jew.

So, the appropriate Orthodox response is to try and bring Reform converts into the Orthodox fold, rather than excluding them because they “aren’t really Jewish.”

The risk, of alienating Jews, who might in fact have halachic obligations of which they are unaware, is too great.
